headline: Stocks slipped from Wednesday's record Dow close as Brent crude jumped 3.8% and the 10-year yield rose to 4.67%, with the July jobs report due Friday after the weakest private-payrolls month in six months.
stance: Into Friday's July jobs report, the tape is being pulled in two directions: hiring data softened all week — 44,000 private-sector jobs added in July, the weakest in six months — while oil re-accelerated, with Brent settling up 3.8% Thursday as the Strait of Hormuz reopening stayed unresolved. Equities eased off Wednesday's record Dow close rather than broke, and credit stayed calm. Friday's print decides whether the roughly 62% market-implied odds of a September hike survive the week.

news.head: Private payrolls miss badly
news.body: Private-sector payrolls data showed just 44,000 jobs added in July versus roughly 75,000 expected — the weakest monthly gain in six months — one day before the official July jobs report.

news.head: Hiring slows, firing doesn't
news.body: Weekly unemployment claims stayed historically low at 199,000 for the week ending August 1 (below forecasts), and announced July job cuts fell 27% from June to the lowest monthly total in two years.

news.head: Oil jumps as a Hormuz deal hangs in the balance
news.body: Brent settled at $82.49 Thursday, up 3.8%; Iran said shipping-route coordinates through the Strait of Hormuz have been agreed with Oman after three weeks of talks, with a joint announcement expected soon — but the strait remains blockaded.

news.head: Dow slips from Wednesday's record
news.body: Thursday's cash session: the Dow fell 0.9% to 53,885.10 a day after its record close, the S&P 500 lost 0.2% to 7,709.96, and the Nasdaq eased 0.1% to 26,348.35 as oil's jump pressured the tape.

news.head: Earnings sort winners from losers
news.body: Honeywell Aerospace fell 23.2% and AppLovin 19.7% Thursday on results that fell short; Warner Bros. Discovery rose 1.7% on a beat — then after the close, Atlassian jumped about 33% and Doximity about 66% on their reports.

news.head: SpaceX rallies through its lockup
news.body: SpaceX rose 6.1% Thursday as a share lockup expired, after trading near all-time lows earlier in the week; Nvidia rose 3% Wednesday after an exclusivity announcement tied to SpaceX.

implications: Friday's jobs print is the swing factor for the front end: futures pricing implies roughly 62% odds of a quarter-point September hike — a soft payrolls number after this week's weak private-sector data would pull that down, while a hot one would cement it with oil already re-tightening the inflation channel.

Thursday paired rising oil with rising yields and falling stocks — the stagflation-flavored mix — but the full week still shows equities up about 3.7% and credit spreads narrower; which picture sticks rides on Friday's data.

A confirmed Hormuz reopening would hit the inflation channel fast: the bond market's 10-year inflation expectation closed Wednesday at just 2.22% against 3.7% realized June inflation — bonds are already betting the energy impulse fades, and a reopening validates that bet while another disruption breaks it.

Positioning: New this week: speculators' Treasury longs reached the 97th percentile of the last three years in 5-year futures and the 87th in 2-year — the bond market has piled into bets that rates fall, a contrarian warning for those notes if payrolls print hot.

watch.head: July jobs report (before Friday's open)
watch.body: Consensus sits near 85,000 jobs (forecast range roughly 80,000–100,000) with unemployment expected at 4.2%–4.3%, against June's 57,000; after the 44,000 private-payrolls miss, this is the week's decisive print.

watch.head: Strait of Hormuz announcement
watch.body: Iran says a shipping-route agreement with Oman is close; a confirmed reopening would relieve the supply squeeze that had Brent up 3.8% Thursday, while no announcement — or a new disruption — keeps the pressure on.

watch.head: Software follow-through at Friday's open
watch.body: Atlassian (~+33%), Doximity (~+66%), Twilio and Cloudflare (~+16% each) all surged in Thursday's after-market on earnings; whether those gains hold at the open is the cleanest read on enterprise-software demand.

watch.head: 10-year yield at 4.67%
watch.body: Thursday's rise came from oil; a hot jobs number on top of it would add pressure on long rates, while a soft one relieves it — the fastest-moving input into equity valuations right now.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: The biggest change since the last brief: the labor market visibly cooled into Friday's July jobs report. Private payrolls rose just 44,000 in July (weakest in six months, versus roughly 75,000 expected) while weekly claims held historically low at 199,000 — an economy hiring less without firing more.
Consensus for Friday's official report is near 85,000 jobs (range roughly 80,000–100,000) with the unemployment rate expected at 4.2%–4.3%, against June's 57,000.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.67% Thursday from Wednesday's 4.63% close as oil jumped; the 2-year closed Wednesday at 4.18%, leaving the curve at +45 basis points (Wednesday's closes).
Futures pricing implies roughly 62% odds of a quarter-point September hike (as of Tuesday–Wednesday) — essentially unchanged from a week ago; Friday's report is the swing factor.

Brent settled at $82.49 Thursday, up 3.8%: Iran said shipping-route coordinates through the Strait of Hormuz have been agreed with Oman after three weeks of talks, but the strait remains blockaded and the joint announcement has not come.
Gold sat at multiweek highs near $4,342 Thursday evening, up from Wednesday's $4,308 close; the 10-year real (inflation-adjusted) yield closed Wednesday at 2.41%.
sections.positioning: New this week: speculators are extended long the belly of the Treasury curve — 5-year futures positioning at the 97th percentile of the last three years, 2-year at the 87th. In plain English: the bond market has piled into bets that rates fall, a contrarian warning for those notes if Friday's jobs number comes in hot.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: Thursday's cash closes: S&P 500 down 0.2% at 7,709.96, Dow down 0.9% at 53,885.10 a day after Wednesday's record close, Nasdaq down 0.1% at 26,348.35 — oil's jump did the damage.
The pullback is small against the week: the S&P 500 remains up about 3.7% from its July 30 close after last week's earnings-driven surge.
Earnings did the sorting Thursday: Honeywell Aerospace fell 23.2% and AppLovin 19.7% on results that fell short; Warner Bros. Discovery added 1.7% on a beat.
After Thursday's close: Atlassian about +33%, Doximity about +66%, Twilio and Cloudflare about +16% each on their reports — early-evening indications, not Friday opening prints.
SpaceX rose 6.1% Thursday as a share lockup expired, after trading near all-time lows earlier in the week; Nvidia rose 3% Wednesday after an exclusivity announcement tied to SpaceX.

Volatility stayed quiet and breadth improved: the VIX held near 15.9 Thursday evening (15.81 at Wednesday's close), tail-risk pricing eased to 133 Wednesday from about 140 a week earlier, and 58% of Nasdaq-100 members now sit above their 50-day trend line versus 49% at the end of July.
sections.positioning: Standing backdrop, not new: speculators have held almost no bullish bets in Russell 2000 futures for 14 straight weeks — a three-year low that acts as a contrarian floor under small caps.

single_name.note: (Columbus McKinnon — construction machinery and lifting gear) - company insiders have been buying, with a fresh purchase filing this week; the shares trade above their 200-day trend line and the setup's dark-pool and options signals are live.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: Credit took the week's rally and Thursday's oil jump in stride: the high-yield-over-investment-grade spread narrowed to 273 basis points (Tuesday's close) from 287 in late July, and investment-grade spreads sit at 78 basis points (Tuesday's close).
Short-term funding is quiet: the key bank-funding spreads closed Wednesday at about 1 basis point, and the commercial-paper funding spread was 25 basis points at end-July — no stress signals.

System liquidity remains ample but the spare cushion is gone: bank reserves stood at $2,984.6 billion and the Treasury's cash account at $910.8 billion (both as of July 29), while the overnight reverse-repo facility — the system's spare-cash pool — is essentially empty at $1.6 billion (Wednesday).

The bond market still treats the oil-driven inflation impulse as temporary: the 10-year breakeven inflation rate closed Wednesday at 2.22% against 3.7% realized June inflation — Thursday's oil move is a direct test of that assumption.
